identity.title: Cool vs warm extremities (cold/wet vs warm profile)

technique.how: With the back of your hand, feel the temperature of the forearms, hands, shins and feet and note the level at which they become cool; add capillary refill, mottling of the knees and pulse pressure. Combine with congestion signs (JVP, orthopnea, oedema) to assign a profile: warm/cold x wet/dry.
technique.prerequisites: Room-temperature environment; note ambient cold, peripheral vascular disease and vasopressor use, which cool the skin independently of cardiac output.

interpretation.positive_finding: Cool extremities in a patient with heart failure suggest low cardiac index but are insensitive (about 20%) with only modest specificity (about 88%); the clinician's global 'cold' profile performs somewhat better and a 'cold' or 'wet' profile at discharge predicts higher 6-month event rates.
interpretation.negative_finding: Warm extremities do not exclude a low cardiac index (LR- about 0.9); most patients with cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 in ESCAPE had warm extremities.
interpretation.pitfalls: Cool skin is common with sepsis-related vasoconstriction, hypovolaemia, cold rooms, peripheral arterial disease and vasopressors; warm extremities in vasodilated septic shock coexist with hypoperfusion. Do not equate 'cold' with a specific cause of shock.
interpretation.changes_what: Cold + wet: consider low-output state; check lactate, urine output, consider inotrope/ICU. Warm: does not exclude low output; use pulse pressure, lactate and echo/POCUS.

estimates.target_condition: Low cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 in advanced heart failure; finding = cool extremities on baseline H&P
estimates.population: 189 patients hospitalised with advanced decompensated HF randomised in the ESCAPE trial who had pulmonary artery catheter measurements; examiners were HF specialists
estimates.reference_standard: Invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 by pulmonary artery catheter
estimates.computed_from: Table 5 prints sensitivity 20%, specificity 88%, positive LR 1.68 and 'negative LR 1.1'; the printed negative LR is the reciprocal (spec/(1-sens) = 0.88/0.80 = 1.10). Conventional LR- = (1-0.20)/0.88 = 0.91 entered.
estimates.location: Table 5 (Utility of history and physical examination in detecting an invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2); columns frequency, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, LR+, LR-, OR, P

estimates.target_condition: COMPOSITE: low cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 in advanced heart failure; finding = clinician's global 'cold' profile (inadequate perfusion judged from the whole H&P)
estimates.population: 188 ESCAPE trial patients with pulmonary artery catheter measurements; profile assigned by HF-specialist investigators at investigator discretion
estimates.reference_standard: Invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 by pulmonary artery catheter
estimates.computed_from: Table 5 prints sensitivity 33%, specificity 86%, LR+ 2.33 and 'negative LR 1.28' (reciprocal form: 0.86/0.67 = 1.28). Conventional LR- = (1-0.33)/0.86 = 0.78 entered.
estimates.location: Table 5, last row; OR 2.97 (95% CI 1.24-7.13), P = 0.02 in text/Results

sources.citation: Drazner MH, Hellkamp AS, Leier CV, Shah MR, Miller LW, Russell SD, Young JB, Califf RM, et al. Value of clinician assessment of hemodynamics in advanced heart failure: the ESCAPE trial. Circ Heart Fail. 2009.

Nohria A, Tsang SW, Fang JC, Lewis EF, Jarcho JA, Mudge GH, Stevenson LW. Clinical assessment identifies hemodynamic profiles that predict outcomes in patients admitted with heart failure. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2003.
Kaplan LJ, McPartland K, Santora TA, Trooskin SZ. Start with a subjective assessment of skin temperature to identify hypoperfusion in intensive care unit patients. J Trauma. 2001.
Stevenson LW, Perloff JK. The limited reliability of physical signs for estimating hemodynamics in chronic heart failure. JAMA. 1989.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use warm extremities to rule out low cardiac output, and do not interpret cool extremities as cardiogenic in a septic, hypovolaemic, hypothermic or vasopressor-treated patient without other evidence.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Cool, mottled extremities with hypotension, rising lactate or oliguria = shock physiology: ICU-level review and definition of the shock type (POCUS) immediately.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: ESCAPE left the criteria for 'cold' to investigator discretion (Methods); no kappa reported. Kaplan 2001 used two intensivists' subjective skin-temperature judgement without agreement statistics (Abstract).

extraction_notes: Direction/units: ESCAPE Table 5 reports LR- in reciprocal form for every row (checked against printed sens/spec for PPP <25%, SBP <90 and cool extremities), so conventional LR- values were recomputed and computed=true set; the printed LR+ values reproduce sens/(1-spec). Text (Results) states cool extremities "were relatively infrequent findings and were not significantly associated with reduced cardiac index" (OR 1.85, 95% CI 0.72-4.78, P = 0.2, Table 5). Nohria 2003 (PMID 12767667) is PROGNOSTIC, not diagnostic, so no estimate was entered: "Profiles B and C increase the risk of death plus urgent transplantation by univariate (hazard ratio [HR] 1.83, p = 0.02) and multivariate analyses (HR 2.48, p = 0.003)" (Abstract); wet-cold profile C was 91/452 = 20% of admissions (Abstract). Kaplan 2001 (surgical ICU, 264 patients) reports group means only: cardiac index "2.9 +/- 1.2 vs. 4.3 +/- 1.2 L/min/m2" cool vs warm and lactate "4.7 +/- 1.5 vs. 2.2 +/- 1.6 mmol/L" (Abstract) — no 2x2, no estimate. Stevenson & Perloff 1989 give accuracy for proportional pulse pressure <25% ("91% sensitivity and 83% specificity for a cardiac index less than 2.2", Abstract), a different sign, cited for context.
